answers.question: E1
text: {link|Nepos makes this a powerful introduction by presenting Hannibal as the greatest general ever to fight Rome, while keeping his Roman readers on his side.}

He begins with {quote|Hannibal, Hamilcaris filius, Carthaginiensis} {translate|‘Hannibal, son of Hamilcar, a Carthaginian’}. {device|This bare list of name, father and nation, with no verb,} {effect|reads like an entry in a record. It introduces Hannibal at once through the father whose hatred he will inherit, and it ends on Carthaginiensis, the word that marks him out as Rome’s great enemy.} {link|The opening is powerful because it is so confident: Nepos assumes the name alone is enough.}

He then makes a bold claim: {quote|non est infitiandum Hannibalem tanto praestitisse ceteros imperatores prudentia, quanto populus Romanus antecedat fortitudine cunctas nationes} {translate|‘it must not be denied that Hannibal surpassed the other generals in skill by as much as the Roman people surpass all nations in courage’}. {device|The litotes non est infitiandum} {effect|makes the praise sound reluctant but unavoidable, as if the facts force it out of Nepos,} {device|and the balanced tanto … quanto comparison} {effect|sets Hannibal above every general exactly as high as Rome stands above every nation. Because Rome is flattered in the same breath, a Roman reader can accept this praise of an enemy.} {link|Hannibal is raised to the level of Rome itself, which gives the introduction its force.}

{quote|quotienscumque cum eo congressus est in Italia, semper discessit superior} {translate|‘as often as he fought with him in Italy, he always came away the winner’}. {device|The pairing of quotienscumque and semper} {effect|allows no exceptions, and the sentence ends on superior, so the last word we hear is his superiority.}

Nepos goes further: {quote|quod nisi domi civium suorum invidia debilitatus esset, Romanos videtur superare potuisse} {translate|‘if he had not been weakened at home by the jealousy of his own citizens, he seems to have been able to defeat the Romans’}. {device|This unreal condition} {effect|imagines Rome defeated, a shocking thought for a Roman reader, which the cautious videtur softens. It also blames Carthage, not Rome, for his failure,} {link|so Hannibal becomes a tragic figure from the very first chapter.} The point is driven home in {quote|multorum obtrectatio devicit unius virtutem} {translate|‘the spite of many overcame the courage of one’}. {device|The antithesis of multorum and unius, and of obtrectatio and virtutem,} {effect|sums up his fate in one short, pointed sentence: one brave man against many petty ones. devicit is the language of the battlefield, so the only victory ever won over Hannibal is won by his own people.}

Finally Nepos turns to his hatred of Rome: {quote|velut hereditate relictum odium paternum erga Romanos} {translate|‘his father’s hatred of the Romans, left to him as if by inheritance’}. {device|The inheritance metaphor} {effect|makes this hatred part of who Hannibal is, handed down like property,} and {quote|ut prius animam quam id deposuerit} {translate|‘that he laid down his life sooner than that hatred’} {device|is hyperbole} {effect|showing how deep it runs.} The chapter ends {quote|numquam destiterit animo bellare cum Romanis} {translate|‘he never stopped waging war on the Romans in spirit’}. {effect|numquam closes on an unbroken war,} {link|so the introduction looks ahead to the whole Life and leaves the reader expecting a relentless enemy.}
answers.commentary: This is a very good response (Level 5). It engages closely with ‘powerful’ throughout, opening with a clear line of argument and linking most points back to it. A wide range of well-selected quotations covers the whole passage, each accurately translated. Features are precisely named and their effects are developed: the litotes makes the praise sound reluctant, the tanto … quanto comparison flatters Rome while raising Hannibal, and devicit is explained as a military word turned against his own people. The point on quotienscumque … semper is well observed but not linked back to the question, and the hyperbole could be developed further, which keeps this just short of full marks.

answers.question: E1
text: {link|Nepos creates a powerful introduction by praising Hannibal very highly.}

He starts with {quote|Hannibal, Hamilcaris filius, Carthaginiensis} {translate|‘Hannibal, son of Hamilcar, a Carthaginian’}. {device|This is very short} {effect|and gets straight to the point, telling us who Hannibal is.}

{quote|si verum est, quod nemo dubitat} {translate|‘if it is true, which no one doubts’} {device|is a parenthesis} {effect|which reassures the Romans that they are the best before he praises Hannibal, so they will not be offended.} He then says {quote|tanto praestitisse ceteros imperatores prudentia, quanto populus Romanus antecedat fortitudine cunctas nationes} {translate|‘he surpassed the other generals in wisdom as much as the Roman people surpass all nations in courage’}. {device|This is a comparison} {effect|which makes Hannibal seem as great as Rome,} {link|which is a powerful way to introduce him.}

{narrative|Nepos then tells us that every time Hannibal fought the Romans in Italy he won, and that he would have beaten them if his own people had not been jealous of him.|This paraphrases two strong sentences. quotienscumque … semper allows no exceptions, and the unreal condition quod nisi … debilitatus esset imagines Rome defeated; quoting them would turn narrative into analysis.} {quote|multorum obtrectatio devicit unius virtutem} {translate|‘the jealousy of many defeated the courage of one’} {device|is an antithesis between many and one} {effect|which makes Hannibal seem like a lone hero.}

{quote|velut hereditate relictum odium paternum} {translate|‘his father’s hatred, left as if by inheritance’} {device|is a metaphor} {effect|showing that he got his hatred of Rome from his father.} {quote|numquam destiterit animo bellare cum Romanis} {translate|‘he never stopped fighting the Romans in his mind’} {device undeveloped|uses the strong word numquam for emphasis.|‘For emphasis’ says nothing about what is emphasised. numquam ends the chapter on an unbroken war with Rome, so the introduction looks ahead to the whole Life.}

{offquestion|Nepos is writing for Romans, and Hannibal was their greatest enemy, so it is surprising that he praises him so much. This shows that Nepos was a fair writer who was willing to praise an enemy.|This drifts into a judgement about Nepos as a writer. The question asks how the opening is powerful, and the parenthesis si verum est, quod nemo dubitat, already quoted, is how Nepos keeps Romans on side.} {quote|ut prius animam quam id deposuerit} {translate|‘that he gave up his life before he gave up that’} {device undeveloped|is hyperbole, which exaggerates.|Exaggeration is what hyperbole means. The point is that Hannibal would sooner die than stop hating Rome, which makes the hatred the driving force of the whole Life.}
{link|Overall Nepos makes this a powerful introduction because he shows Hannibal as a great general and a lifelong enemy of Rome.}
answers.commentary: This is a good response (Level 4), at the bottom of the level. It engages with the question, covers the whole passage, and quotes and translates sensibly throughout. The points on the parenthesis si verum est, quod nemo dubitat and on the antithesis of multorum and unius are well made. Elsewhere the development is thinner: the comparison is just called ‘a comparison’ with no mention of tanto … quanto, the opening is ‘very short’ without saying why that makes it powerful, and the hyperbole and numquam are named without their effect. One paragraph retells the victories in Italy (quotienscumque … semper would have repaid attention), and the comment on Nepos as a fair writer drifts from the question. More precise naming of features, and fuller explanation of their effect, would lift this into Level 5.

answers.question: E1
text: {link|Nepos makes this a powerful introduction because he shows that Hannibal was a great general and a big enemy of Rome.} {offquestion|Hannibal is one of the most famous generals in history, and he fought against Rome in the Second Punic War, which lasted from 218 to 201 BC. Nepos wrote lots of lives of famous generals, and Hannibal is one of the few who was not Greek.|Background about the war and Nepos’ other Lives says nothing about how this passage makes the introduction powerful. The time would be better spent on the opening words themselves.}

{narrative|At the start Nepos tells us that Hannibal was the son of Hamilcar and that he was a Carthaginian. He then says that if it is true that the Roman people were better than every other nation in courage, then Hannibal was better than every other general in skill.|This retells the first two sentences. The striking points are in the Latin: the bare list Hannibal, Hamilcaris filius, Carthaginiensis, and the litotes non est infitiandum, which makes the praise sound unavoidable.} Nepos uses the word {isolated|imperatores|A single word with no context. The phrase it belongs to, tanto praestitisse ceteros imperatores prudentia, is where the comparison with Rome happens.}, which means {mistranslation|‘emperors’, which shows that Hannibal was more important than all the emperors.|imperatores here means ‘generals’. There were no Roman emperors in Hannibal’s time, so the point drawn from it is wrong as well as the translation.}

{narrative|Then Nepos says that whenever Hannibal fought the Romans in Italy he always won, and that if the people at home had not been jealous of him, he would have defeated the Romans.|What Nepos says is reported without being quoted. quotienscumque … semper and the unreal condition quod nisi … debilitatus esset are the language that makes this powerful.} {offquestion|This is surprising because the Romans did win the war in the end, at the battle of Zama, where Scipio defeated Hannibal.|Zama is not in this passage, and the outcome of the war does not show how Nepos makes this opening powerful.} There is {device undeveloped|an antithesis|The device is correctly named, and the answer stops there. It needs to say what the contrast does: one brave man set against many jealous ones makes Hannibal’s fall seem unjust.} in {quote|multorum obtrectatio devicit unius virtutem}, {undeveloped|which is very effective.|‘Very effective’ could be said of any device. Say what effect it has on the reader and how that makes the introduction powerful.}

{isolated|odium|One word on its own. velut hereditate relictum odium paternum carries the point, because the inheritance metaphor makes hatred of Rome part of who Hannibal is.} means ‘hatred’, and this shows Hannibal hated the Romans. {narrative|He hated them because his father did, and he kept on hating them all his life, even after he was driven out of his country and had to rely on other people’s money.|Paraphrase again. The hyperbole ut prius animam quam id deposuerit, that he gave up his life sooner than his hatred, is what makes this powerful, and it is not mentioned.}

{offquestion|Hannibal is also famous for bringing elephants over the Alps, and many people think he was a better general than any Roman. Even today his battles are studied in military academies.|This may be true, but it is not in the passage and does not answer the question.}
{link|Overall, this is a powerful introduction because we learn that Hannibal is a great general and an important enemy of Rome, so we want to read on.}
answers.commentary: This is a limited response (Level 2), in the middle of the level. It is a full-length answer, but most of it either retells the passage in English or brings in background from outside it (the Punic Wars, Zama, the Alps), none of which shows how Nepos makes the introduction powerful. Only one Latin phrase is quoted; elsewhere single words are picked out (imperatores, odium), and imperatores is mistranslated as ‘emperors’, which leads to a point that cannot be right. The antithesis in multorum obtrectatio devicit unius virtutem is correctly spotted, but ‘very effective’ is not development. There is some engagement with the question at the start and the end, and occasional support from the passage.

answers.question: E2c
text: {link|Nepos makes the oath scene both vivid and solemn by letting Hannibal tell it himself, and by surrounding a small boy’s promise with the full weight of religion.}

The story is told in direct speech: {quote|pater meus inquit Hamilcar} {translate|‘my father Hamilcar,’ he said}. {device|Switching into Hannibal’s own words} {effect|makes the scene vivid, as if we are hearing a memory first-hand, and placing pater meus first frames the oath as a family matter, a debt owed to a father.} He then fixes the moment precisely: {quote|puerulo me, utpote non amplius VIIII annos nato} {translate|‘when I was a little boy, being no more than nine years old’}. {device|The diminutive puerulo and the exact age} {effect|let us picture how small he was, which makes what follows all the more striking: a lifelong oath is laid on a child.}

The setting is religious from the start: {quote|Iovi optimo maximo hostias immolavit} {translate|‘he sacrificed victims to Jupiter Best and Greatest’}. {device|The full formal title of Jupiter, with its two superlatives,} {effect|sounds like the language of ritual itself and places the scene at an altar before the greatest of the gods.} {quote|quae divina res dum conficiebatur} {translate|‘while this sacred rite was being carried out’} {effect|keeps the sacrifice in front of us: everything that follows happens in the middle of it,} {link|so the oath is sworn under the gods’ eyes, which makes it solemn.}

Against this solemn background Nepos sets the boy’s excitement: {quote|id cum libenter accepissem atque ab eo petere coepissem ne dubitaret ducere} {translate|‘when I had gladly accepted this and had begun to beg him not to hesitate to take me’}. {device|The eager libenter and the pleading petere coepissem} {effect|bring the boy to life, and his excitement about going on campaign contrasts sharply with the grave condition his father is about to set,} {link|which makes the scene vivid and human.}

Hamilcar’s reply is brief: {quote|faciam, inquit, si mihi fidem, quam postulo, dederis} {translate|‘“I will,” he said, “if you give me the pledge that I demand”’}. {device|It opens with the single decisive word faciam, and the conditional} {effect|turns a father’s promise into a contract; postulo, ‘I demand’, is stern and formal.} The action follows at once: {quote|simul me ad aram adduxit} {translate|‘at the same moment he led me to the altar’}. {effect|simul quickens the pace, as if the boy has no time to think,} and {quote|eamque ceteris remotis tenentem} {translate|‘holding it, with everyone else sent away’} {device|adds a physical detail and a private setting:} {effect|we see the boy’s hands on the altar, alone with his father, so the moment feels both intimate and sacred.}

Finally, {quote|iurare iussit numquam me in amicitia cum Romanis fore} {translate|‘he ordered me to swear that I would never be on terms of friendship with the Romans’}. {device|The alliteration of iurare iussit} {effect|gives the command a ritual ring, and numquam makes the oath absolute and lifelong;} {link|the scene ends on its most solemn words, an oath that will shape the rest of Hannibal’s life.}
answers.commentary: This is an excellent response (Level 5, full marks). Both parts of the question are addressed throughout: vividness (the direct speech, the diminutive puerulo, the boy’s eagerness, the physical detail of holding the altar) and solemnity (the formal title of Jupiter, divina res, the stern postulo, the absolute numquam). Quotations are well selected from every part of the passage and accurately translated, and each feature is explained in terms of its effect as well as named. The contrast between the boy’s excitement and his father’s grave demand is a perceptive point that shows real engagement with the scene. Not every point needs to be this full to reach the top of the level, but the range and precision here are exemplary.

answers.question: E2c
text: {link|Nepos makes the scene vivid by using direct speech.} {quote|pater meus inquit Hamilcar} {translate|‘my father Hamilcar,’ he said} {effect|is in direct speech, which makes it more vivid because we hear it from Hannibal himself.}

{quote|puerulo me} {translate|‘me as a little boy’} {effect|shows that Hannibal was very young, which makes the scene sad.} {offquestion|Children in the ancient world grew up much faster than today, and many boys went to war very young.|General history of childhood is not in the passage. The diminutive puerulo and the precise age are what matter: a lifelong oath is laid on a small child.}

{narrative|Hannibal explains that when he was nine years old his father was going to Spain as a general and made a sacrifice to Jupiter before he left.|This passes over the most solemn language in the scene: Iovi optimo maximo hostias immolavit and quae divina res dum conficiebatur set the oath inside a sacrifice.} {quote|Iovi optimo maximo} {translate|‘to Jupiter best and greatest’} {device undeveloped|uses superlatives,|The superlatives are Jupiter’s formal cult title, optimus maximus. Saying that this ritual language places the oath before the greatest of the gods would explain why the scene is solemn.} {link|which makes it solemn.}

{quote|quae divina res dum conficiebatur} {translate|‘while this divine thing was being done’} {effect|shows that the sacrifice was still going on,} {undeveloped|which makes it solemn.|The right phrase, and then the answer stops. Say why it matters that the oath is sworn during a sacrifice: it puts the promise under the eyes of the gods.}

{isolated|libenter|One word quoted alone. id cum libenter accepissem atque ab eo petere coepissem shows the boy’s eagerness and begging, which contrasts with the grave condition his father sets.} means ‘gladly’ and shows that Hannibal really wanted to go with his father, {effect|which makes him seem like a real child.}

Hamilcar says {quote|faciam, inquit, si mihi fidem, quam postulo, dederis} {translate|‘I will do it, he said, if you give me the faith which I ask for’}. {effect|This is direct speech again, which makes it vivid, and it shows that Hamilcar is serious.}

{offquestion|Hamilcar seems like a strict father, and it is cruel to make a nine-year-old boy promise something so serious. Most fathers today would not do this.|A modern judgement on Hamilcar as a parent does not answer how Nepos makes the scene vivid or solemn.} {narrative|Hannibal was very eager to go and agreed straight away.|This repeats an earlier point in English.}

{narrative|Then he took him to the altar, sent everyone else away, and made him hold the altar and swear.|The climax is narrated. simul me ad aram adduxit and eamque ceteris remotis tenentem give the speed, the private setting and the boy holding the altar, which make the scene vivid and sacred.} {quote|numquam me in amicitia cum Romanis fore} {translate|‘that I would never be in friendship with the Romans’} {device|uses numquam,} {effect|which shows how strong the oath was and that it would last for ever.} {link|This makes the scene solemn because it is a very serious promise.}
answers.commentary: This is a reasonable response (Level 3), towards the top of the level. It has a clear point about direct speech, made twice, and some development of the oath itself through numquam. However, it leans heavily on vividness and says little about how the scene is made solemn: the superlatives and divina res are called solemn without any explanation of why, when the religious setting of the sacrifice and the altar would have given plenty to discuss. Two paragraphs simply narrate the story, a point is repeated, libenter is picked out as a single word, and the comment on Hamilcar as a parent drifts from the question. Translation is generally accurate. Some development and a selection of examples lead to tenable conclusions.

text: {narrative|In this passage Hannibal is telling the story of how his father Hamilcar took him to Spain when he was nine years old. Before they left Carthage, Hamilcar made a sacrifice to Jupiter, and while it was happening he asked Hannibal if he wanted to come to the camp with him. Hannibal said yes and begged his father to take him.|A summary of the opening. Hannibal’s own words, pater meus inquit, and the precise age, puerulo me, utpote non amplius VIIII annos nato, are what make the scene vivid, and neither is quoted.} {undeveloped|This is vivid.|‘Vivid’ is asserted with no evidence. libenter and petere coepissem would show the boy’s eagerness.}

{offquestion|Hamilcar Barca was a famous Carthaginian general who fought in the First Punic War in Sicily. After Carthage lost that war, he went to Spain to build up an empire there, because he wanted revenge on the Romans.|Hamilcar’s career is not in the passage and does not show how Nepos makes the oath scene vivid or solemn.}

{isolated|aram|A single word. simul me ad aram adduxit and eamque ceteris remotis tenentem would let you discuss the altar, the private setting and the boy’s hands on it.} means ‘altar’, which is solemn because it is religious. {narrative|Hamilcar took him to the altar, sent everyone else away, and made him hold the altar and swear that he would never be friends with the Romans.|Retelling. The command iurare iussit and the absolute numquam are where the solemnity lies.} {isolated|iurare|Another single word. Quote the whole oath, iurare iussit numquam me in amicitia cum Romanis fore, and explain what numquam does.} means ‘to swear’.

{mistranslation|Hamilcar says that he will take him if Hannibal gives him the faith he demands, which shows that Hamilcar wanted Hannibal to believe in the gods.|fidem here means a pledge, a promise of loyalty. The scene turns on the boy giving his word to his father, and religious belief has nothing to do with it.}

{offquestion|This oath was very important because Hannibal kept it all his life. He crossed the Alps with elephants and won great battles like Cannae, where he killed thousands of Romans, and later he even fought against the Romans for King Antiochus.|The rest of Hannibal’s life is not in this passage. The question asks how this scene is made vivid and solemn.} {offquestion|In the end he killed himself with poison so that he would not be handed over to the Romans, which shows that he never broke the oath.|More from outside the passage. His death does not help with the oath scene.}

{undeveloped|Nepos also uses direct speech, which makes it vivid, and there are lots of long sentences, which makes it solemn.|Two features named with no example and no explanation. Quote pater meus inquit or faciam, inquit and say what hearing the words does for the scene; long sentences are not solemn in themselves.}
{link|So the scene is vivid and solemn because it is the start of Hannibal’s hatred of Rome and it shows how important religion was to the Carthaginians.}
answers.commentary: This is a very limited response (Level 1), at the top of the level. It is long, but nearly all of it is narrative paraphrase or background from outside the passage: Hamilcar’s career, the Alps, Cannae and Hannibal’s death do nothing to answer a question about this scene. The only Latin is two single words (aram, iurare); no phrase is quoted or analysed and no literary feature is identified. fidem is misread as religious faith, which leads to a point the passage does not support. ‘Vivid’ and ‘solemn’ are asserted, never shown. A start would be to quote and translate a whole phrase such as Iovi optimo maximo hostias immolavit and explain what the formal language adds.

answers.question: E4b
text: {link|Nepos makes the crossing of the Alps seem heroic by stressing how great an obstacle the mountains were, by comparing Hannibal with Hercules, and by showing his relentless effort.}

He builds up to the Alps: {quote|saltum Pyrenaeum transiit} {translate|‘he crossed the Pyrenean pass’}. {device|This short, plain statement} {effect|makes crossing a whole mountain range sound routine, which prepares us for a far greater feat.} {quote|neminem nisi victum dimisit} {translate|‘he let no one go unless defeated’} {device|is an emphatic negative} {effect|showing that nothing on the march could stop him,} {link|so he arrives at the Alps already unbeaten.}

The Alps themselves are a barrier between nations, {quote|quae Italiam ab Gallia seiungunt} {translate|‘which separate Italy from Gaul’}, and {quote|quas nemo umquam cum exercitu ante eum praeter Herculem Graium transierat} {translate|‘which no one had ever crossed with an army before him except Hercules the Greek’}. {device|The strong negatives nemo umquam and the comparison with Hercules} {effect|put Hannibal in the company of a mythical hero: only a demigod had done this before,} {link|which makes his achievement heroic in the literal sense.} {quote|quo facto is hodie saltus Graius appellatur} {translate|‘because of which that pass is today called the Graian pass’} {effect|reminds us that Hercules’ feat is still remembered in a place name, implying that Hannibal’s deserves the same lasting fame.}

{quote|Alpicos conantes prohibere transitu concidit} {translate|‘he cut down the Alpine tribesmen who tried to stop him crossing’}. {device|The violent verb concidit} {effect|shows him removing human obstacles as forcefully as natural ones.} Then {quote|loca patefecit, itinera muniit, effecit} {translate|‘he opened up the ground, he built roads, he brought it about’}: {device|the asyndeton of three short verbs in the perfect} {effect|conveys relentless, practical labour, one achievement after another,} {link|so the heroism lies in engineering as well as fighting.}

{quote|ut ea elephantus ornatus ire posset, qua antea unus homo inermis vix poterat repere} {translate|‘that an equipped elephant could go along the route where before one unarmed man could scarcely crawl’}. {device|The contrast between the huge, laden elephant and one unarmed man, stressed by vix and repere,} {effect|measures how much he has changed the mountains.} {quote|hac copias traduxit in Italiamque pervenit} {translate|‘by this route he led his forces across and reached Italy’} {effect|is a short, calm ending: the goal is reached without fuss.}
answers.commentary: This is a very good response (Level 5), at the bottom of the level. It has a clear argument, covers the whole passage, and quotes accurately with good translations. The Hercules comparison is well developed, and the point about the place name is perceptive. The asyndeton of loca patefecit, itinera muniit, effecit is precisely analysed and linked to the question. Some later points are less fully linked to ‘heroic’: the striking contrast of the elephant and the man who could barely crawl is identified, but the answer does not draw out what it says about Hannibal, and the final point is brief. Those small gaps keep the mark at 13.

answers.question: E4b
text: {link|Nepos presents the crossing of the Alps as a heroic achievement in several ways.}

{quote|quas nemo umquam cum exercitu ante eum praeter Herculem Graium transierat} {translate|‘which no one had ever crossed with an army before him except Greek Hercules’}. {device|Nepos compares Hannibal to Hercules,} {effect|a great hero of mythology, so Hannibal seems like a hero too,} {link|and the crossing seems almost superhuman because only Hercules had done it.}

{quote|quo facto is hodie saltus Graius appellatur} {translate|‘because of this the pass is called Graian today’} {undeveloped|tells us something interesting about the name of the pass.|‘Interesting’ is not an effect. The place name keeps Hercules’ feat alive, which suggests that Hannibal’s deserves the same lasting fame.} {offquestion|Hercules was famous for his twelve labours, such as killing the Nemean lion and cleaning the Augean stables.|The labours are outside knowledge and do not show how Nepos makes the crossing heroic.}

{quote|Alpicos conantes prohibere transitu concidit} {translate|‘he killed the Alpine people who were trying to stop him crossing’} {effect|shows that he had to fight as well as cross the mountains, which makes it harder and so more heroic.}
{quote|loca patefecit, itinera muniit} {translate|‘he opened up places, he built roads’} {device|is asyndeton} {effect|which makes it sound as if he did a lot of work quickly.}

{quote|elephantus ornatus ire posset, qua antea unus homo inermis vix poterat repere} {translate|‘an equipped elephant could go where before one unarmed man could hardly crawl’}. {device|This is a contrast between the elephant and the man} {effect|which shows how difficult the route was before Hannibal changed it, and how much he achieved.} {link|This is the most heroic part of the passage.}

{narrative|At the start of the passage Nepos tells us that Hannibal divided his army into three, sent one part to Africa, left one in Spain and took one to Italy, and that he crossed the Pyrenees and fought everyone on the way.|This retells the opening, and puts it last. neminem nisi victum dimisit and the plain saltum Pyrenaeum transiit build up to the Alps and could have been analysed.} {link|Overall the crossing seems heroic because it was so difficult.}
answers.commentary: This is a good response (Level 4), at the top of the level. Its main points are relevant and accurately supported: the Hercules comparison, the fighting with the Alpine tribes and the contrast of the elephant with the crawling man are all explained in terms of the question. The range is narrower than in the best answers, though: the opening of the passage is only narrated, so neminem nisi victum dimisit and the plain saltum Pyrenaeum transiit are missed, the asyndeton gets only a brief comment on speed, and the place name is found ‘interesting’ without any effect. The labours of Hercules add nothing to the answer. Wider coverage and fuller analysis would take it into Level 5.

answers.question: E4b
text: {link|Nepos makes the crossing of the Alps seem a heroic achievement because it was very difficult and dangerous.} {offquestion|The Alps are the highest mountains in Europe and are covered in snow for most of the year, so crossing them with an army of thousands of men and horses, as well as elephants, would have been extremely hard.|General knowledge about the Alps. The passage gives its own evidence of the difficulty, especially qua antea unus homo inermis vix poterat repere.}

{narrative|At the start of the passage Hannibal splits his army into three parts. He sends one to Africa, leaves one in Spain with his brother Hasdrubal, and takes one with him to Italy. Then he crosses the Pyrenees and fights all the people who live there.|Retelling. neminem nisi victum dimisit, with its emphatic negative, would show that he arrives at the Alps unbeaten.}

{narrative|Then Nepos tells us that Hannibal came to the Alps, which separate Italy from Gaul, and that no one had crossed them with an army before except Hercules.|The best point in the passage is paraphrased. Quoting quas nemo umquam cum exercitu ante eum praeter Herculem Graium transierat would let you discuss the strong negatives and the comparison.} {effect|This makes Hannibal seem as great as Hercules, who was the greatest hero of Greek myth.}

{narrative|The Alpine tribes tried to stop him, but he killed them.|The sentence this paraphrases, Alpicos conantes prohibere transitu concidit, has a violent verb worth discussing: he removes human obstacles as forcefully as natural ones.} {isolated|concidit|A single word, and misread. Alpicos conantes prohibere transitu concidit shows him cutting down the tribes who tried to block him.} means {mistranslation|‘he fell’, which shows that the crossing was dangerous even for Hannibal and that he nearly died.|concidit here is from concīdo, ‘cut down’: Hannibal cuts down the tribesmen. Reading it as ‘he fell’ produces a point the passage does not support.}

There is {device undeveloped|a tricolon|Correctly named, then left. The three short verbs in asyndeton convey relentless, practical effort, which is part of what makes the feat heroic.} in {quote|loca patefecit, itinera muniit, effecit}, {undeveloped|which emphasises what he did.|‘Emphasises’ explains nothing. Say what is emphasised and how it makes the crossing seem heroic.}

{narrative|He made it possible for an elephant to go where a man could barely crawl before, and then he took his army into Italy.|The best contrast in the passage, told only in English. Quoting elephantus ornatus … unus homo inermis vix poterat repere would let you show the scale of what he did.} {offquestion|Many of the elephants died in the snow, and Hannibal lost a large part of his army on the way.|This is not in the passage, and it does nothing to show how Nepos presents the feat.}

{offquestion|Hannibal was only about twenty-nine when he did this, which makes it even more heroic.|Hannibal’s age is not in the passage, and it says nothing about how Nepos presents the crossing.} {undeveloped|Nepos also uses a lot of verbs, which shows Hannibal was busy.|A vague observation with no Latin. loca patefecit, itinera muniit, effecit was already quoted: explain what the asyndeton does.}
{link|Overall Nepos shows that the crossing was heroic because Hannibal did something nobody except Hercules had done.}
answers.commentary: This is a limited response (Level 2), at the top of the level. It is a full-length answer, but much of it narrates the passage or adds general knowledge about the Alps and the elephants, which does not show how Nepos presents the achievement. It makes one sound point, that the comparison with Hercules makes Hannibal seem great, though from English paraphrase. concidit is mistranslated as ‘he fell’ (here it is from concīdo, ‘cut down’), which leads to a point the passage does not support. The tricolon is correctly identified and quoted, but ‘emphasises what he did’ does not explain its effect, and the excellent contrast of the elephant and the crawling man is mentioned only in English.

answers.question: E6
text: {link|Nepos presents Hannibal as a master of cunning by showing him escape a trap through an ingenious trick, and then use deceit again and again to destroy Rome’s commanders.}

{quote|hic clausus locorum angustiis noctu sine ullo detrimento exercitus se expedivit} {translate|‘trapped here by the narrowness of the terrain, he got himself out at night without any loss to his army’}. {device|The contrast between clausus near the start and se expedivit at the end} {effect|shows him turning an impossible position into an escape, and sine ullo detrimento stresses how complete it was.}

{quote|Fabioque, callidissimo imperatori, dedit verba} {translate|‘and he tricked Fabius, a most cunning commander’}. {device|The superlative callidissimo} {effect|praises Fabius as the cleverest of generals in the very clause in which Hannibal fools him, so Hannibal seems cleverer still. The idiom dedit verba, literally ‘gave words’, is itself the language of trickery.}

{quote|sarmenta in cornibus iuvencorum deligata incendit} {translate|‘he set fire to bundles of twigs tied to the horns of young bullocks’}. {effect|The precise detail makes the trick vivid and shows how inventive it was.} {quote|quo repentino visu obiecto tantum terrorem iniecit exercitui Romanorum, ut egredi extra vallum nemo sit ausus} {translate|‘by presenting this sudden sight he struck such terror into the Roman army that no one dared to go outside the rampart’}. {device|The result clause, ending on nemo sit ausus,} {effect|shows a whole Roman army pinned down by a few burning cattle,} {link|which shows the power of his cunning.}

He uses the same skill against others: {quote|dolo productum in proelium fugavit} {translate|‘having lured him into battle by a trick, he routed him’}, and Gracchus was killed {quote|absens in insidias inductum} {translate|‘led into an ambush while Hannibal was absent’}. {effect|absens suggests that his cunning works even at a distance.} {quote|pari modo interfecit} {translate|‘he killed him in the same way’} {effect|shows that ambush is his usual method.}

{quote|nemo ei in acie restitit, nemo adversus eum post Cannensem pugnam in campo castra posuit} {translate|‘no one stood against him in battle, no one pitched camp against him in the open after the battle of Cannae’}. {device|The anaphora of nemo} {effect|emphasises that the Romans no longer dared to face him.}
answers.commentary: This is a good response (Level 4), at the top of the level. It is well organised and focused on ‘cunning’, with a range of accurate quotations and translations from the whole passage. The analysis of callidissimo, praising Fabius just as he is fooled, is perceptive, and the point that a whole army is pinned down by the trick is well developed. The later points are thinner: absens and pari modo are noted briefly, and the titles of the Roman victims (magistrum equitum pari ac dictatorem imperio, quinquies consulem), which make each deception more impressive, are not discussed. The final point on the anaphora of nemo is not linked to cunning at all. With these developed, the answer would reach Level 5.

answers.question: E6
text: {link|Nepos shows that Hannibal was very cunning.} {quote|Fabioque, callidissimo imperatori, dedit verba} {translate|‘he deceived Fabius, the cleverest general’}. {device|callidissimo is a superlative} {effect|which shows that Fabius was clever, but Hannibal was even cleverer because he tricked him.}

{quote|hic clausus locorum angustiis} {translate|‘shut in here by the narrowness of the places’} {effect|shows that Hannibal was trapped, which makes his escape more impressive.} {narrative|He got out at night without losing any of his army.|sine ullo detrimento exercitus is worth quoting: the escape was complete, which is part of the cunning.}

{narrative|Hannibal tied twigs to the horns of cattle, set them on fire, and let the cattle loose at night.|The trick itself is told in English. sarmenta in cornibus iuvencorum deligata incendit is vivid detail worth quoting, and it shows how inventive the trick was.} {quote|tantum terrorem iniecit exercitui Romanorum} {translate|‘he threw so much terror into the Roman army’} {device|has alliteration of t} {undeveloped|which emphasises the terror.|‘Emphasises the terror’ only restates the words. The point is that a few burning cattle pin down a whole Roman army (ut egredi extra vallum nemo sit ausus), which shows the power of his cunning.} {effect|The Romans were too scared to leave their camp, which shows how well the trick worked.}

{quote|dolo productum in proelium fugavit} {translate|‘he put him to flight, having led him into battle by a trick’} {effect|shows that he used tricks against Minucius as well.} {narrative|He also killed Gracchus in an ambush and Marcellus in the same way.|absens in insidias inductum and pari modo are clear evidence of cunning: he works even at a distance, and ambush is his usual method. Here they are only narrated.}

{quote|M. Claudium Marcellum, quinquies consulem} {translate|‘Marcus Claudius Marcellus, five times consul’} {undeveloped|tells us how important Marcellus was.|True, and it could go further: killing a five-times consul pari modo, by the same kind of ambush, shows his cunning beating Rome’s most experienced men.}

{offquestion|Hannibal’s most famous victory was at Cannae, where he surrounded the Roman army and killed most of it. This was also cunning, because he let his centre fall back and then attacked from the sides.|Cannae appears in the passage only as a date. The tactics described come from outside it and earn no credit.} {quote|longum est omnia enumerare proelia} {translate|‘it would take a long time to list all the battles’} {device undeveloped|is a praeteritio,|Named and left. Nepos claims there are too many battles to list, which suggests endless victories; the answer should say how that adds to the picture of Hannibal.} {effect|which shows that he won many battles.}
{link|This shows that Hannibal was a master of cunning because he beat many Roman generals with tricks.}
answers.commentary: This is a reasonable response (Level 3), at the top of the level. It stays mostly focused on cunning and makes some good points: the trap of clausus makes the escape more impressive, callidissimo makes Hannibal’s deception of Fabius more impressive, and dolo productum shows deceit used again. Translations are sound. Elsewhere the development is limited: the trick with the cattle is narrated, the alliteration point stops at ‘emphasises’, the deaths of Gracchus and Marcellus are told in English when absens and pari modo offered clear evidence of cunning, and the praeteritio is named without its effect. The paragraph on the tactics at Cannae comes from outside the passage. Fewer, more fully developed points would move it into Level 4.

answers.question: E6
text: {narrative|In this passage Hannibal is trapped in a narrow place but he manages to escape at night without losing any of his army.|Retelling. clausus … se expedivit is the contrast that shows his cunning getting him out of a trap.} {offquestion|Fabius was a Roman general who was called Cunctator, the Delayer, because he refused to fight Hannibal in a pitched battle. Instead he followed him around Italy and wore him down, and in the end his tactics worked and Rome won the war.|Outside knowledge about Fabius. The passage’s own point is that Hannibal fooled callidissimo imperatori, the most cunning of commanders.}

{narrative|Hannibal tied sticks to the horns of cattle and set them on fire. Then he drove the cattle at the Romans in the night. The Romans were very frightened and did not leave their camp.|The trick is narrated without any Latin. tantum terrorem … ut egredi extra vallum nemo sit ausus shows a whole army pinned down by it.} {offquestion|This is a famous story which is also told by Livy, who says that there were two thousand cattle.|Livy’s version is not in the passage and does not show how Nepos presents Hannibal’s cunning.}

{narrative|After this Hannibal beat Minucius, who had the same power as the dictator. Then he killed Gracchus in Lucania and Marcellus at Venusia.|Each of these defeats comes with a word of cunning in the Latin (dolo productum, absens in insidias inductum, pari modo), and none is quoted.} {isolated|insidias|One word. absens in insidias inductum shows his cunning working even when he was not there.} {translate|means ‘ambush’.}

{undeveloped|Nepos uses lots of names of Roman generals in this passage, which makes it more detailed.|The names come with titles (magistrum equitum pari ac dictatorem imperio, quinquies consulem) that make each defeat more impressive. ‘More detailed’ does not say that, and it is not linked to cunning.} {offquestion|Gracchus was from a famous family, and later two of the Gracchi brothers became tribunes and tried to give land to the poor.|The later Gracchi have nothing to do with this passage.}

{offquestion|Marcellus was a very famous Roman general who had captured Syracuse, where the scientist Archimedes was killed by a Roman soldier.|Syracuse and Archimedes have nothing to do with this passage or with Hannibal’s cunning.}

{undeveloped|The passage is very fast because a lot of things happen.|Speed is asserted with no Latin. The list of victims, each dealt with in a short clause ending on fugavit, sustulit or interfecit, would show it, and it would still need linking to cunning.}

{offquestion|Hannibal was a great general because he never lost a battle in Italy, and nobody dared to fight him after Cannae, where he killed about fifty thousand Romans in one day.|The end of the passage is about the Romans’ fear of him, and the casualty figures come from outside it. Neither is about cunning.} {link|So he was very cunning.}
answers.commentary: This is a very limited response (Level 1). It is a long answer, but almost none of it addresses the question. It shows a general understanding of what happens, yet no Latin is quoted beyond the single word insidias, and no literary feature is identified. Large parts come from outside the passage (Fabius’ tactics, Livy’s figures, Marcellus at Syracuse, the casualties at Cannae) and gain no credit. The last paragraph is about Hannibal’s success in general, with the link to cunning only asserted in the final sentence. To improve, the answer needed to quote and translate phrases such as dedit verba or dolo productum and explain how they show deceit.

answers.question: E11
text: {link|Nepos makes the story entertaining by setting up a contest of wits between the cleverest of men and the greedy Cretans, letting the reader in on the trick, and ending with a comic reversal.}

{quote|vidit autem vir omnium callidissimus} {translate|‘but this man, the cleverest of all, saw’}. {device|The superlative, strengthened by omnium,} {effect|announces Hannibal as a trickster before we know what he will do, so we read on expecting something clever.} Against him stand the Cretans: {quote|propter avaritiam Cretensium} {translate|‘because of the greed of the Cretans’}. {effect|Defining them by their greed makes them deserve what is coming,} {link|so the reader can enjoy seeing them fooled.}

{quote|itaque capit tale consilium} {translate|‘so he forms the following plan’}. {device|This short sentence in the historic present, with tale pointing forward,} {effect|builds anticipation, like a storyteller pausing before the trick.} {quote|amphoras complures complet plumbo, summas operit auro et argento} {translate|‘he fills several jars with lead and covers the tops with gold and silver’}. {device|The asyndeton and the historic presents} {effect|make the preparations quick and concrete, and the alliteration of complures complet gives a playful sound. The contrast between cheap lead below and gold and silver on top is the whole joke in miniature.}

{quote|has praesentibus principibus deponit in templo Dianae} {translate|‘he deposits these in the temple of Diana in the presence of the leading men’}. {device|The alliteration of p} {effect|draws attention to the solemn audience, and the temple setting makes it funnier: the leading citizens are formally witnessing a sham.} {quote|simulans se suas fortunas illorum fidei credere} {translate|‘pretending that he was entrusting his fortune to their good faith’}. {effect|simulans lets us in on the pretence, and fidei is ironic, since it is the Cretans’ lack of good faith that he fears.} {link|We share the joke with Hannibal, which is what makes the story entertaining.}

Meanwhile {quote|statuas aeneas … omni sua pecunia complet easque in propatulo domi abicit} {translate|‘he fills bronze statues with all his money and throws them down in the open courtyard of his house’}. {device|abicit, ‘throws down’,} {effect|makes the real treasure seem carelessly tossed aside, an audacious bluff.}

{quote|Gortynii templum magna cura custodiunt non tam a ceteris quam ab Hannibale} {translate|‘the people of Gortyn guard the temple with great care, not so much against others as against Hannibal’}. {device|The non tam … quam construction} {effect|delivers the punchline: they guard lead against the very man who left it,} {quote|ne ille inscientibus iis tolleret sua} {translate|‘in case he took away his own property without their knowledge’}, {effect|while his money lies in full view.} {link|The comic reversal makes the greedy Cretans look foolish and gives the story its entertaining ending.}
answers.commentary: This is a very good response (Level 5). It shows a clear grasp of what makes the episode entertaining (the contest of wits, the reader’s share in the secret, the reversal) and builds the answer around it. Quotation is plentiful and accurate, covering the passage from the first line to the last, and features are explained precisely: the storyteller’s pause in capit tale consilium, the irony of fidei, and the punchline of non tam … quam. The statues are linked to the bluff but not back to the question, and the alliteration points are light, but this is a convincing and well-supported answer.

answers.question: E11
text: {link|The story is entertaining because Hannibal tricks the Cretans.} {narrative|Hannibal was worried because he had a lot of money and the Cretans were greedy, so he made a plan.|vir omnium callidissimus and propter avaritiam Cretensium set up a contest of wits; quoting them would show how the story is made entertaining from its first line.}
{quote|vir omnium callidissimus} {translate|‘the most cunning man of all’} {device|is a superlative} {effect|which shows that Hannibal is very clever, so we expect him to trick the Cretans.}

{quote|amphoras complures complet plumbo} {translate|‘he fills many jars with lead’} {device|is in the historic present,} {effect|which makes it more vivid and exciting.} {narrative|He put gold and silver on top and left the jars in the temple of Diana in front of the leading men.|has praesentibus principibus deponit in templo Dianae stages the sham in a temple before the leading men, which is part of the comedy. Paraphrase loses it.}

{offquestion|The Cretans had a reputation in the ancient world for being liars, so it is ironic that Hannibal lies to them.|Outside knowledge about Cretans. The irony inside the passage is in fidei: he pretends to trust the good faith of greedy men.} {quote|in templo Dianae} {translate|‘in the temple of Diana’} {undeveloped|is a religious place, which makes it more serious.|The temple setting makes the sham funnier, because the leading men are solemnly witnessing a fake. ‘More serious’ points the wrong way for a question about entertainment.}
{quote|simulans se suas fortunas illorum fidei credere} {translate|‘pretending that he trusted his fortune to their faith’} {effect|shows that he is lying to them, which is funny.}

{narrative|He put his real money in bronze statues and left them at his house.|statuas aeneas … in propatulo domi abicit is the audacious bluff: the real money is tossed into the open courtyard. abicit is worth discussing.} {isolated|custodiunt|One word picked out of the key sentence. Gortynii templum magna cura custodiunt non tam a ceteris quam ab Hannibale is the punchline of the story.} means {mistranslation|‘they keep it for themselves’, which shows the Cretans were greedy.|custodiunt means ‘they guard’. The Cretans guard the temple against Hannibal himself, which is the comic reversal, and this reading loses it.}
{narrative|In the end Hannibal’s money was safe and the Cretans were guarding jars full of lead.|This is the joke, stated without the Latin that delivers it: non tam a ceteris quam ab Hannibale.}

{narrative|The Cretans were happy because they thought they had Hannibal’s money, and they did not know about the statues.|This narrates what the Cretans believe. Nepos carries the irony in his in errorem inductis, ‘with them led into error’, which is worth quoting.} {undeveloped|Nepos uses lots of details in this story, which makes it more entertaining.|Which details, and why do they entertain? The lead hidden under gold and silver is the whole joke in miniature, and saying so would be a point.}
{link|This is entertaining because the Cretans think they have Hannibal’s money but they only have lead.}
answers.commentary: This is a reasonable response (Level 3), at the bottom of the level. It understands the trick and makes some relevant points: callidissimus is rightly seen as setting up a clever trick, the historic present is identified, and simulans shows deception. Much of the answer narrates, though, the points are brief, and the temple is said to make the scene ‘more serious’, which works against the question. custodiunt is misunderstood as the Cretans keeping the money for themselves, when Nepos says they guard the temple against Hannibal, so the comic reversal of non tam a ceteris quam ab Hannibale, the heart of the entertainment, is missed. The remark about Cretans as liars comes from outside the passage. The conclusion is tenable but rests on paraphrase.

answers.question: E11
text: {narrative|Hannibal went to Crete with a lot of money. He was worried because the Cretans were very greedy and he knew they had heard about his money.|Retelling. vir omnium callidissimus and propter avaritiam Cretensium set up a contest between the cleverest of men and greedy opponents, which is where the entertainment starts.} {offquestion|He had come to Crete because he had to escape after the Romans defeated King Antiochus, and the Romans wanted Hannibal handed over to them.|Background from outside the passage. {offquestion|Diana was the goddess of hunting and the moon, and her temple was a holy place.|Facts about Diana do not help. The temple matters because the leading men are solemnly witnessing a fake, which makes the scene comic.}

answers.commentary: This is a limited response (Level 2), at the bottom of the level. It tells the story accurately and at length, but almost entirely in English paraphrase. The only Latin is the single word callidissimus, labelled a superlative with no comment on its effect. Background on Antiochus and the episodes with Fabius and Eumenes come from outside the passage and gain no credit. non tam … quam is misread, so the comic reversal at the end, which is the heart of the entertainment, is missed. The answer never explains why the trick is entertaining: the reader’s knowledge of the pretence (simulans) and the irony of the Cretans guarding lead were there to be discussed.

answers.question: E16b
text: {link|Nepos makes Hannibal’s last moments dramatic by slowly closing a trap around him, showing the danger through the eyes of a boy, and ending on Hannibal’s calm choice of death.}

{quote|huc cum legati Romanorum venissent ac multitudine domum eius circumdedissent} {translate|‘when the Roman envoys had come here and had surrounded his house with a large force’}. {device|The two pluperfect verbs} {effect|tell us that the trap is already set before the scene begins, so the reader knows more than Hannibal does,} {link|which creates dramatic irony and tension.}

{quote|puer ab ianua prospiciens Hannibali dixit plures praeter consuetudinem armatos apparere} {translate|‘a boy looking out from the door told Hannibal that more armed men than usual were appearing’}. {device|Seeing the danger through the eyes of a boy} {effect|makes the scene immediate, and praeter consuetudinem quietly signals that something is wrong.}

{quote|ut omnes fores aedificii circumiret ac propere sibi nuntiaret, num eodem modo undique obsideretur} {translate|‘to go round all the doors of the building and quickly report to him whether he was being besieged on every side in the same way’}. {device|The urgent propere and the indirect question} {effect|keep us waiting with Hannibal for the answer,} and the reply comes fast: {quote|puer cum celeriter, quid esset, renuntiasset omnesque exitus occupatos ostendisset} {translate|‘when the boy had quickly reported what was happening and shown that all the exits were occupied’}. {device|celeriter, echoing propere,} {effect|speeds up the narrative, and omnes exitus occupatos closes every escape at once.}

{quote|sensit id non fortuito factum, sed se peti} {translate|‘he realised that this had not happened by chance, but that he was the target’}. {device|The antithesis of non fortuito and se peti} {effect|marks the moment of realisation,} {link|the turning point of the drama.} {quote|neque sibi diutius vitam esse retinendam} {translate|‘and that he must not keep his life any longer’} {effect|follows at once, without hesitation.}

{quote|quam ne alieno arbitrio dimitteret, memor pristinarum virtutum} {translate|‘so as not to give it up at another’s will, remembering his former courage’}. {effect|He chooses to keep control of his fate, which makes the death dignified,} and {device|the sentence holds back its main verb to the very end:} {quote|venenum, quod semper secum habere consuerat, sumpsit} {translate|‘he took the poison which he had always been in the habit of keeping with him’}. {effect|sumpsit is the last word of the scene, so the drama ends on his final act.}
answers.commentary: This is a very good response (Level 5), at the bottom of the level. It is carefully structured around the build-up of tension, and the observation that the pluperfects let the reader know about the trap before Hannibal does is perceptive. Quotations are accurate and well chosen from the whole passage, and the pairing of propere and celeriter is a neat point about pace. The final paragraph is strong on the placing of sumpsit, though semper (he had carried the poison all along) could have been developed. A few points stop at the effect without returning to ‘dramatic’, which keeps the mark at 13.

It could only earn credit if linked to the irony that here, for once, there is no way out, and that link is not made.} {quote|puer ab ianua prospiciens} {translate|‘a boy looking out from the door’} {undeveloped|shows that a boy saw the soldiers first.|The answer notices the boy and stops. {quote|sensit id non fortuito factum, sed se peti} {translate|‘he realised this had not happened by chance, but that he was being sought’}. {device|This is an antithesis} {effect|which shows the moment when Hannibal realises what is happening.}

{offquestion|It is sad that such a great general had to die like this, alone in a foreign country.|Sympathy for Hannibal is a fair response, but the question asks how Nepos makes the moments dramatic, and this is not linked to the language.} {isolated|celeriter|A single word. In puer cum celeriter, quid esset, renuntiasset it answers Hannibal’s propere, and the pair speed the scene up.} means ‘quickly’, {effect|which shows that the boy hurried.}

answers.commentary: This is a good response (Level 4), at the bottom of the level. It works through the whole passage with relevant, accurately translated quotations and keeps the focus on drama: the sense of being trapped, the unusual number of armed men, the moment of realisation. The development is uneven: the antithesis is named and only briefly explained, propere is quoted as a single word, the boy at the door is noticed without its effect, and the last sentence asserts that the ending is dramatic without showing how Nepos makes it so (the delay of sumpsit, the significance of semper). The comparison with the escape from Fabius drifts from the passage. Fewer, more fully developed points would serve it better.

answers.question: E16b
text: {link|Nepos makes Hannibal’s last moments dramatic because Hannibal is trapped and has to kill himself.} {offquestion|By this point Hannibal was an old man living in Bithynia with King Prusias, and the Romans had sent Flamininus to demand that Prusias hand him over.|Context from outside this passage. The drama is in how Nepos tells the scene itself, starting with the house surrounded multitudine.}

{narrative|The Romans came to Hannibal’s house and surrounded it with lots of soldiers. A boy at the door saw them and told Hannibal that there were more armed men than usual. Hannibal told him to go round all the doors and see if the house was surrounded, and the boy came back quickly and said all the exits were blocked.|A long retelling. propere and celeriter speed the scene up and omnes exitus occupatos closes every escape, and none of this is quoted.} {link|This is dramatic because Hannibal is trapped.}
{quote|sensit id non fortuito factum} {translate|‘he felt that this was not done by luck’} {effect|shows that Hannibal realised what was happening.}

{quote|neque sibi diutius vitam esse retinendam} {mistranslation|‘and that his life would not be held for long’|The gerundive retinendam means his life must not be kept: Hannibal decides for himself that he should no longer live. Reading it as a prediction removes his choice from the scene.} {mistranslation|shows that he knew he was going to be killed by the Romans.|This follows from the mistranslation. The next words, ne alieno arbitrio dimitteret, show the opposite: he dies so as not to be at the mercy of anyone else.}

There is {device undeveloped|a lot of suspense|‘Suspense’ is named with no example. The indirect question num eodem modo undique obsideretur keeps us waiting with Hannibal for the boy’s report.} in this passage, {undeveloped|which makes it dramatic.|This restates the question. Show how the suspense is created, then link it to drama.} {offquestion|It is like a scene in a film where the hero is surrounded by his enemies.|A comparison with films does not analyse Nepos’ language.}

{isolated|venenum|One word. venenum, quod semper secum habere consuerat, sumpsit is the whole final act, with sumpsit held to the end.} means ‘poison’, {undeveloped|which is dramatic.|Calling a word dramatic is not analysis. Say how Nepos makes the moment dramatic: he delays the verb, and semper reveals he was always prepared.}
{offquestion|Some writers say that Hannibal’s last words were a complaint that the Romans were afraid of an old man.|This comes from other sources, not this passage, and gains no credit.}

{narrative|In the end Hannibal took the poison that he always carried with him and died.|The ending is told in English. sumpsit is held back to the very end of the sentence, and semper shows he had been ready for this all along.} {offquestion|He was about seventy years old, and he had been fighting the Romans for most of his life, ever since he swore the oath to his father.|Not in this passage, and it does not show how these moments are made dramatic.} {link|This is a dramatic ending to his life.}
answers.commentary: This is a limited response (Level 2), at the top of the level. There is clear engagement with ‘dramatic’ and the idea of a trap, and two phrases are quoted. However, much of the length is narrative or background (Prusias, Flamininus, Hannibal’s age, a comparison with films) that does not show how Nepos makes the scene dramatic. The gerundive in neque sibi diutius vitam esse retinendam is mistranslated: Nepos says Hannibal decided he must no longer keep his life, which is his own choice, and the misreading hides the most important point about the ending. ‘Suspense’ is mentioned without any example of how it is created. Points such as the boy’s view from the door or the delay of sumpsit to the end of the sentence would have raised the level.

drills.question: E5
drills.latin: utriusque exercitus uno proelio fugavit, Paulum consulem occidit et aliquot praeterea consulares
drills.weak: Nepos uses the word occidit (‘killed’), which shows that Hannibal was violent.
drills.strong: utriusque exercitus uno proelio fugavit, Paulum consulem occidit et aliquot praeterea consulares (‘he routed the armies of both in a single battle, and killed the consul Paulus and several ex-consuls besides’): uno proelio set against utriusque exercitus makes Cannae one crushing blow, the asyndeton of fugavit and occidit piles up the results, and the ranks of the dead, a consul and several ex-consuls, show how much of Rome’s leadership fell at once, so the victories seem overwhelming.
drills.why: A single word with an obvious meaning shows nothing about Nepos’ writing. Quoting the whole phrase brings in uno proelio and the ranks of the dead, which is where the overwhelming effect lies.

drills.question: E15
drills.latin: postquam autem naves suas oppletas conspexerunt serpentibus, nova re perterriti
drills.strong: postquam autem naves suas oppletas conspexerunt serpentibus, nova re perterriti (‘but after they saw their ships filled with snakes, utterly terrified by this new thing’): serpentibus is held back to the end of its clause, so the reader discovers the snakes at the same moment as the sailors, and the strong compound perterriti marks the sudden switch from laughter to panic, which makes the moment dramatic.
drills.why: Knowing what one word means is not analysis. The drama comes from where Nepos puts the word and what it does to the sailors.

drills.question: E7b
drills.latin: pulsus incredibile dictu biduo et duabus noctibus Hadrumetum pervenit
drills.weak: After losing at Zama, Hannibal travelled to Hadrumetum in two days and two nights, which was three hundred miles away. Then the Numidians ambushed him but he beat them.
drills.strong: pulsus incredibile dictu biduo et duabus noctibus Hadrumetum pervenit (‘beaten, incredible to say, he reached Hadrumetum in two days and two nights’): the single participle pulsus disposes of the defeat in one word, Nepos’ aside incredibile dictu shares his own amazement with the reader, and the precise biduo et duabus noctibus makes the speed concrete, so the narrative races on as fast as Hannibal does.
drills.why: Retelling what happens gains no credit by itself. The stronger version picks out how Nepos tells it: the brevity, the aside and the precise detail.

drills.question: E9
drills.latin: bona eius publicarunt, domum a fundamentis disiecerunt, ipsum exulem iudicarunt
drills.weak: The Carthaginians sent two ships after him, took his property, knocked down his house and made him an exile.
drills.strong: bona eius publicarunt, domum a fundamentis disiecerunt, ipsum exulem iudicarunt (‘they confiscated his property, tore his house down from its foundations, and declared him an exile’): the asyndetic tricolon, each clause ending on a perfect verb, makes the punishments fall one after another; a fundamentis shows a spite that goes beyond justice, and the climax on ipsum exulem turns from his possessions to the man himself, which seems all the more unjust after his careful service to the treasury.
drills.why: The weak point is an accurate summary, and that is all it is. The stronger version shows how the shape of the sentence makes the punishment seem excessive.

drills.question: E14
drills.latin: Hannibal, ut palam faceret suis, quo loco Eumenes esset, tabellarium in scapha cum caduceo mittit
drills.weak: Hannibal sent a messenger in a boat to find out where Eumenes was.
drills.strong: Hannibal, ut palam faceret suis, quo loco Eumenes esset, tabellarium in scapha cum caduceo mittit (‘to make clear to his men where Eumenes was, Hannibal sends a messenger in a small boat with a herald’s staff’): the vivid historic present mittit and the details of the little boat and the herald’s staff, the sign of a peace envoy, let us see the disguise; the purpose clause tells us the real aim first, so we watch the enemy trust the messenger knowing what he is for, which makes the trick entertaining.
drills.why: Narrative tells the reader what happened; the question asks how Nepos makes it entertaining. Here the answer is that he lets us into the secret before the enemy.

drills.question: E14
drills.latin: statim ad Eumenem deductus est, quod nemo dubitabat, quin aliquid de pace esset scriptum
drills.weak: statim ad Eumenem deductus est uses the word statim, which emphasises it.
drills.strong: statim ad Eumenem deductus est, quod nemo dubitabat, quin aliquid de pace esset scriptum (‘he was immediately taken to Eumenes, because no one doubted that something about peace had been written’): statim shows how easily the enemy is fooled, and the irony of nemo dubitabat entertains the reader, who knows the letter holds only insults while everyone on Eumenes’ side takes it for a peace offer.
drills.why: ‘Emphasises it’ explains nothing. Say what is emphasised and why that matters to the question.

drills.question: E5
drills.latin: qua valetudine cum etiam tum premeretur lecticaque ferretur, C. Flaminium consulem apud Trasumenum cum exercitu insidiis circumventum occidit
drills.weak: Nepos uses a cum clause here to show that Hannibal was ill.
drills.strong: qua valetudine cum etiam tum premeretur lecticaque ferretur, C. Flaminium consulem apud Trasumenum cum exercitu insidiis circumventum occidit (‘while he was still weighed down by this illness and being carried in a litter, he trapped the consul Gaius Flaminius and his army in an ambush at Trasimene and killed him’): the cum clause shows Hannibal at his weakest, half-blind and carried in a litter, and sets this against the destruction of a consul and his whole army, so even sick he cannot be beaten, and the victories seem overwhelming.
drills.why: Naming the grammar is not the same as analysing it. The point is what the illness adds to the victory.

drills.question: E17
drills.latin: sic vir fortissimus, multis variisque perfunctus laboribus, anno acquievit septuagesimo
drills.weak: vir fortissimus is a superlative, which emphasises how brave he was.
drills.strong: sic vir fortissimus, multis variisque perfunctus laboribus, anno acquievit septuagesimo (‘so this bravest of men, having come through many and varied labours, found rest in his seventieth year’): the superlative fortissimus gives Nepos’ final verdict, multis variisque … laboribus recalls the whole life the reader has just followed, and acquievit, ‘found rest’, is a gentle word for a death by poison, so the Life closes on peace after struggle, a fitting end for a hero.
drills.why: The weak point names the superlative and repeats its meaning. The stronger version sets it in the whole sentence and links it to ‘fitting close’.

drills.question: E14
drills.latin: at Eumenes soluta epistula nihil in ea repperit, nisi quae ad irridendum eum pertinerent
drills.weak: Eumenes was the king of Pergamum, which was an ally of Rome, and this is why Hannibal was fighting him.
drills.strong: at Eumenes soluta epistula nihil in ea repperit, nisi quae ad irridendum eum pertinerent (‘but when Eumenes opened the letter he found nothing in it except things meant to mock him’): the king, expecting a peace offer, finds only insults; nihil … nisi and ad irridendum make mockery the letter’s whole purpose, and after nemo dubitabat the let-down is all the funnier, which is what makes the trick entertaining.
drills.why: Background about Pergamum may be true, but it does not answer how Nepos makes the trick entertaining. Every point should be about the passage and the question’s key word.

drills.question: E9
drills.latin: in eo magistratu pari diligentia se Hannibal praebuit, ac fuerat in bello
drills.weak: Hannibal was a brilliant general who crossed the Alps and won at Cannae, so it is unjust that he was exiled.
drills.strong: in eo magistratu pari diligentia se Hannibal praebuit, ac fuerat in bello (‘in that office Hannibal showed the same diligence as he had in war’): Nepos stresses that he served Carthage just as well in peace, and the non solum … sed etiam that follows shows him paying Rome and still leaving a surplus, so when his own city confiscates his property and destroys his house, the punishment seems shockingly unjust.
drills.why: The Alps and Cannae are not in this passage. The passage gives its own evidence of his service to Carthage, and the point should come from that.

drills.question: E15
drills.latin: quae iacta initio risum pugnantibus concitarunt
drills.weak: quae iacta initio risum pugnantibus concitarunt means ‘which, thrown at the start, made the fighters run’, so they were scared at once.
drills.strong: quae iacta initio risum pugnantibus concitarunt (‘when these were thrown, at first they made the fighting men laugh’): risum is laughter, and initio marks it as only the first reaction; the Pergamenes’ amusement at a few clay pots sets up the drama, because moments later the laughter turns to terror when the snakes appear.
drills.why: risum (laughter) was taken for a verb of running. The misreading reverses the point: the drama comes from the change from laughter to panic.

drills.question: E7b
drills.latin: quos non solum effugit, sed etiam ipsos oppressit
drills.weak: quos non solum effugit, sed etiam ipsos oppressit means ‘he not only fled from them but was also oppressed by them’, which shows how much he suffered.
drills.strong: quos non solum effugit, sed etiam ipsos oppressit (‘he not only escaped them but even overpowered them’): oppressit is active, with Hannibal as its subject and ipsos as its object; non solum … sed etiam builds to a climax, so even an ambush during a retreat ends in his victory, which keeps the passage fast-moving and vivid.
drills.why: oppressit is an active verb: Hannibal does the overpowering. Getting the voice wrong turns his triumph into suffering.
